q: The points are (0, 0), (3, 4), (6, 1), (7, 5), (10, 2), (11, 7). What is the square of the smallest distance between any two of them?
explain:
Squared distances of the nearby pairs:

(0,0)-(3,4):  9 + 16 = 25
(3,4)-(6,1):  9 + 9  = 18
(3,4)-(7,5): 16 + 1  = 17
(6,1)-(7,5):  1 + 16 = 17
(6,1)-(10,2): 16 + 1 = 17
(7,5)-(10,2): 9 + 9  = 18
(7,5)-(11,7): 16 + 4 = 20

The minimum squared distance is 17, reached by three different pairs. Its square root is about 4.12.

q: The closest-pair algorithm is run with the strip re-sorted by y at every level (no presorting). Its recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c·n log n. If T(n) = Θ(n logᵏ n), what is k?
explain:
Each of the log n levels does about c·n log n work (n points spread over 2ⁱ subproblems, each sorting n/2ⁱ points):

Σ over levels of n·log(n/2ⁱ) ≈ n·(log n + (log n − 1) + …) = Θ(n log² n)

So k = 2. Presorting removes one log factor, giving O(n log n).

q: Why does the closest-pair algorithm compare each strip point with only a constant number of others?
options: Points within the same half are at least δ apart, so few can fit in a δ × 2δ rectangle
The strip always has at most 7 points
Distances in the strip are all equal
Because the points are sorted by x
explain: δ is the smallest distance within each half, so points on the same side of the line are at least δ apart. Packing such points into a δ × 2δ box allows at most 8 in total. So after sorting by y, only the next 7 can be within δ.

q: For the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm on n points, which statements are true?
options: With presorting, it runs in O(n log n)
Its recurrence has the same form as merge sort's
It examines every pair of points at least once
It is an example of divide and conquer where the combine step is the main difficulty
explain:
(A) and (B): T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). (D): splitting is trivial, and the clever part is combining with the strip check.

(C) is false: avoiding examining every pair is the whole point.
